lessons.title: **Course Orientation** — Trace what this course explains, why it matters, and where its model ends.
**Internet History** — Explain the relationship between packet networking, open protocols, and the Web's development.
**Internet and Web** — Distinguish network infrastructure from applications built on it.
**Web Resources** — Distinguish pages, websites, applications, documents, and referenced resources.
**Client and Server** — Explain request/response responsibility without assuming every server is a web framework.
**Standards and Interoperability** — Relate published protocols and browser variation to compatible delivery.
**The Web Journey** — Sketch a first device-to-visible-page model with identified unknown steps.
**Network Interfaces** — Explain link media and the roles of interfaces on a connected device.
**Local Networks** — Distinguish wireless access, Ethernet, switches, and routers.
**IP Configuration** — Explain host addresses, DHCP, default gateways, and basic NAT.
**Internet Access** — Relate last-mile connections, ISPs, and upstream networks.
**Packets and Frames** — Distinguish link-layer delivery from IP datagrams and packet forwarding.
**IPv4 Addresses** — Interpret addresses, prefixes, and local versus routed destinations.
**IPv6 Addresses** — Interpret basic IPv6 address and prefix structure without assuming IPv4 behavior.
**Routing Decisions** — Read a route and next hop; explain forwarding and hop-limit consequences.
**Network Measurements** — Distinguish latency, bandwidth, throughput, jitter, loss, and their evidence limits.
**Connectivity Failures** — Classify link, gateway, routing, ICMP, and upstream symptoms using safe observations.
**Ports and Sockets** — Relate transport endpoints and listeners to IP addressing.
**TCP Handshakes** — Trace a connection attempt at a conceptual level.
**TCP Streams** — Explain ordering, retransmission, and why an application must define message boundaries.
**Connection Failures** — Distinguish refusal, reset, timeout, and the limitations of each observation.
**UDP Datagrams** — Compare datagram delivery with TCP's reliable stream semantics.
**QUIC and HTTP/3** — Explain why QUIC uses UDP while providing transport features to HTTP/3.
**Connection Reuse** — Relate latency, multiplexing, and protocol choices without treating them as identical.
**Loopback and Dual Stack** — Explain local listener tests and IPv4/IPv6 address-family differences.
**Domain Names** — Explain human-readable labels, subdomains, and the DNS namespace.
**DNS Hierarchy** — Distinguish root, top-level domains, and delegated zones.
**Domain Registration** — Trace registrant, registrar, registry, ICANN, renewal, transfer, and expiration roles.
**Nameserver Delegation** — Explain how delegated authority differs from owning a website or hosting it.
**DNS Resolvers** — Distinguish local stub, recursive, and authoritative resolvers.
**Resolution Walkthrough** — Trace referrals, records, caching, and the resulting answer.
**DNS Records** — Interpret A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, and the limited role of MX.
**DNS Caching** — Explain TTLs, positive/negative caching, stale answers, and hosts-file overrides.
**DNS Failures** — Distinguish NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, timeout, and local cache effects.
**DNS Observation Limits** — Explain why a local or browser lookup does not prove a public-network query and where DoH/privacy affects visibility.
**Web Hosting** — Distinguish hosted files/content, servers, and domain-name services.
**Static and Dynamic** — Compare static resource delivery with dynamically produced responses conceptually.
**Hosting Models** — Compare shared hosting, virtual machines, managed hosting, and serverless at a high level.
**Origin Servers** — Relate a listening HTTP process to an origin and its hosted resources.
**Reverse Proxies** — Explain intermediated requests and origin visibility.
**CDN Edges** — Explain geographically distributed delivery and shared caching boundaries.
**Load Balancing** — Trace requests among origin instances and describe availability limitations.
**Delivery Paths** — Distinguish DNS answers, origin identity, intermediary responses, and the actual serving location.
**Resource Identifiers** — Explain why addresses identify resources and what a URL does not guarantee.
**URL Components** — Parse scheme, authority, hostname, port, path, query, and fragment.
**Relative URLs** — Resolve paths against a document or declared base URL.
**Encoding and Names** — Explain percent encoding, Unicode domain-name concepts, and ambiguous interpretation.
**Browser Origins** — Derive origins from scheme, host, and port.
**Sites and Domains** — Distinguish registrable sites, subdomains, and origins.
**Navigation Targets** — Predict how redirects, changed paths, and fragment-only navigation affect requests.
**HTTP Exchange** — Interpret the application-layer request and response model.
**Message Structure** — Explain request targets, fields, bodies, and representation metadata.
**Request Methods** — Distinguish GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE semantics.
**Safety and Idempotence** — Separate protocol method properties from application retry behavior.
**Response Status** — Classify successful, redirected, client-error, and server-error responses.
**Representations** — Interpret Content-Type, negotiation, compression, and body-length constraints.
**Authority and Headers** — Explain the request's target authority and selected headers.
**HTTP Versions** — Distinguish shared HTTP semantics from HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 framing and transport.
**Cache Purposes** — Distinguish browser/private caches, shared caches, and origin responses.
**Freshness Controls** — Interpret Cache-Control, freshness lifetime, no-store, and private scope.
**Cache Validators** — Explain ETag and Last-Modified as representation validation mechanisms.
**Conditional Requests** — Trace If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, and 304 Not Modified decisions.
**Redirect Behavior** — Interpret redirect locations, status codes, and follow-up requests.
**Cache Keys** — Explain Vary, representation differences, and why a URL alone may be insufficient.
**Intermediary Effects** — Distinguish cache hits, proxy behavior, and origin observability.
**Storage Boundaries** — Separate HTTP caching from browser application storage and persistent content.
**HTTPS Guarantees** — Explain protected transport and the risks of plaintext HTTP.
**TLS Handshake** — Describe negotiated cryptography and authenticated key establishment conceptually.
**Certificate Chains** — Explain trust anchors, issuers, and certificate validation.
**Hostname Verification** — Relate requested host identity to a certificate without equating it to content honesty.
**Protocol Negotiation** — Explain SNI and ALPN at an appropriate introductory level.
**TLS and QUIC** — Distinguish TLS use with TCP-based HTTPS and HTTP/3 over QUIC.
**Mixed Content** — Explain security warnings, downgrade risks, and secure-context boundaries.
**Trust Failures** — Classify supplied certificate/hostname errors without bypassing browser validation.
**Browser Responsibilities** — Identify UI, navigation, networking, rendering, and device interaction roles.
**Browser Processes** — Explain conceptual process separation, threads, and sandbox boundaries.
**Rendering Engines** — Distinguish Blink, Gecko, and WebKit as engine implementations.
**JavaScript Engines** — Distinguish V8, SpiderMonkey, and JavaScriptCore from layout/rendering engines.
**Engine Variations** — Explain how shared standards coexist with implementation differences.
**Site Isolation** — Explain why browsers isolate potentially untrusted content.
**Browser Inspection** — Relate developer-tool observations to engine behavior without unsupported generalization.
**Navigation Lifecycle** — Trace address entry, history, navigation decisions, and document commitment.
**Connections and Redirects** — Relate redirects and existing connections to navigation timing.
**Document Streaming** — Explain incremental arrival and discovery of document content.
**Resource Discovery** — Explain how stylesheets, images, fonts, and scripts are requested.
**Preload and Priority** — Describe speculative discovery and relative resource scheduling at a high level.
**Blocking Behavior** — Distinguish parser-blocking scripts, deferred/async loading, and render-blocking stylesheets.
**Readiness Milestones** — Distinguish load events, first paint, and interactive readiness conceptually.
**Network Waterfalls** — Interpret request ordering, reuse, caching, and failure evidence in browser tools.
**HTML Decoding** — Explain byte/character decoding and tokenization at a conceptual level.
**DOM Construction** — Trace tree building and common parser recovery effects.
**DOM Representation** — Distinguish the DOM from source bytes and rendered boxes.
**CSS Parsing** — Explain declarations, rule parsing, and error recovery.
**Selector Matching** — Trace a simple selector to affected elements.
**Cascade and Inheritance** — Explain why competing style declarations produce specific computed values.
**Computed Styles** — Inspect an element's computed styling and distinguish it from authored CSS.
**Semantics and Accessibility** — Relate meaningful document structure to the accessibility tree without requiring authoring mastery.
**Rendered Boxes** — Distinguish the box/render representation from DOM nodes.
**Layout Constraints** — Explain geometry, containing blocks, and basic formatting context.
**Text and Viewports** — Relate font metrics and viewport changes to layout results.
**Paint Order** — Explain painting instructions, stacking, and visible order.
**Rasterization** — Explain conversion of paint operations into pixels.
**Compositing** — Explain compositing layers and conceptual GPU responsibilities.
**Incremental Rendering** — Describe what changes can require style, layout, paint, or compositing work.
**Visual Diagnostics** — Identify layout shifts, missing styles, and delayed paint using controlled comparisons.
**Same-Origin Policy** — Explain default cross-origin access restrictions.
**CORS Boundaries** — Explain controlled permission for cross-origin reads, not a way to bypass transport rules.
**Cookies and Sessions** — Distinguish cookie state and conceptual session identifiers.
**Browser Storage** — Compare local storage, HTTP caches, and service-worker-controlled resources.
**Secure Contexts** — Explain mixed content, permission prompts, and trustworthy-context restrictions.
**Web Attack Concepts** — Recognize CSRF, credential handling, and untrusted-content boundaries without implementing backend authentication.
**Privacy and Evidence** — Protect browsing histories, credentials, local data, and observation context.
**Security Diagnostics** — Distinguish TLS, CORS, HTTP, permission, and storage symptoms using available evidence.
**The Complete Journey** — Explain how connection, name resolution, transport, HTTP, parsing, and rendering connect.
**Failure Boundaries** — Classify link/routing, DNS, transport, TLS, HTTP, resource, parsing, and visual failures.
**Static-Site Fixtures** — Prepare or inspect a controlled HTML/CSS/image site using an unprivileged local server.
**Evidence Collection** — Record request traces, document/style observations, tool versions, and uncertainty.
**Controlled Failures** — Compare four distinct fault cases and explicit nonfault controls.
**Repair Verification** — Apply narrow safe changes and re-run observations to verify at least two repairs.
**Diagnostic Defense** — Present a reproducible Internet-to-pixels explanation and justified next observations.

outcomes.description: Distinguish Internet infrastructure, the World Wide Web, browsers, resources, clients, servers, and intermediaries, and explain their responsibilities in a complete website visit.
Trace local connectivity, IPv4/IPv6 addressing, packet forwarding, routing, and observable network failure boundaries using appropriately qualified evidence.
Explain ports, TCP connection and stream behavior, UDP datagrams, QUIC fundamentals, and the relationship between transport and HTTP versions.
Trace domain registration, DNS delegation and resolution through resolvers and caches, interpreting record types, TTLs, and common failure responses.
Distinguish domain names, hosted content, origin servers, reverse proxies, CDNs, load balancers, and distributed content-delivery paths.
Parse and resolve URLs and explain schemes, authority, ports, paths, queries, fragments, browser origins, and the distinction between origin and site.
Interpret HTTP messages, request methods, response codes, representation headers, redirects, caching, validators, and the behavior of intermediaries.
Explain HTTPS and TLS negotiation, certificate-chain and hostname validation, protocol selection, mixed-content behavior, and the limits of connection trust.
Compare browser, renderer, networking, graphics, and JavaScript-engine responsibilities, including process isolation and implementation differences.
Trace navigation and incremental document/resource loading, identifying blocking and deferred resources and interpreting browser network waterfalls.
Explain HTML parsing, DOM creation, CSS parsing, selector matching, the cascade, computed styles, and the distinction between document and accessibility representations.
Trace the visible rendering pipeline through style resolution, layout, paint, rasterization, and compositing, diagnosing representative delays or visual changes.
Classify same-origin and CORS boundaries, cookies, browser storage and caching, secure contexts, mixed content, permissions, and relevant privacy risks.
Investigate an unfamiliar static website's network-to-pixels behavior, reproduce and classify failures, apply safe repairs, and defend observed versus inferred evidence.
